title: How to Lead When You Are Not in Charge
subtitle: A guide for the associate pastor, the staff member, and the volunteer on leading up under authority you did not choose, influencing without title, and serving faithfully when the final decision belongs to someone else.

sections.title: Most Leadership Happens Here
sections.body:
We picture leadership as the corner office and the final word. That picture is a lie for almost everyone who has ever led anything.

Most leadership happens from the middle. The associate who carries a vision he did not set. The youth director answering to an elder board. The volunteer who sees the problem clearly and has no authority to fix it. The staff member who could improve the whole ministry if only someone would let her. This is where the actual work of the church gets done, by people who are not in charge and lead anyway.

David led for years before he ever wore a crown. He commanded men in the wilderness, won loyalty, made decisions that shaped a kingdom, all while serving a king who was actively trying to kill him. He was a leader long before he had the authority to match. So was Joseph in Potiphar's house. So was Daniel in a pagan court. So was Nehemiah, a cupbearer with a burden and no jurisdiction.

If you are waiting to be in charge before you start leading, you have misunderstood the assignment. The middle is not the waiting room for leadership. The middle is where most of it lives.

sections.title: Influence Is Earned, Not Granted
sections.body:
When you have a title, people do what you say because of the title. When you do not, they do what you say because of who you are. The second is harder to build and far harder to lose.

Influence without authority is bought with competence and character over time. You become the person whose opinion is asked because your opinions have proven sound. You become the one consulted before decisions because your judgment earned a seat no one formally gave you. This cannot be demanded. It can only be deposited, slowly, until one day the people in charge cannot imagine deciding without you.

Joseph did not seize authority in Egypt. He simply became so trustworthy that authority kept getting handed to him. Potiphar stopped checking his work. The prison warden stopped supervising him. Pharaoh put the nation in his hands. The blessing of the Lord was on him, and so was a track record no one could ignore.

The leader in the middle does not lobby for influence. He becomes the kind of person influence accrues to, and then he uses it carefully, because he knows how long it took to earn and how fast a single self-serving move would spend it all.

sections.title: How to Lead Up Without Undermining
sections.body:
Leading up is the most misunderstood skill in ministry. Most people do it badly in one of two directions. Some never push at all, swallowing every disagreement until they are bitter and useless. Others push constantly, treating every difference as a hill, until their leader stops listening to anything they say.

The faithful middle leader does neither. He brings his honest read to the person in charge, privately, fully, without flinching. Then, when the decision goes the other way, he supports it publicly as if it were his own, because it now is. Disagree in the room. Unite outside it. The leader who reverses that order, agreeing to your face and undermining behind your back, is not leading up. He is running a quiet rebellion.

Nathan confronted David, a king with the power to kill him, and did it so wisely that David convicted himself before he understood he was the target. That is leading up. Not cowardice, which says nothing. Not insubordination, which says everything loudly to everyone. Courage aimed precisely at the one person who needed to hear it, delivered in a way he could actually receive.

If you cannot disagree with your leader to his face and back him to everyone else, you are not yet ready for authority of your own.

sections.title: Guard Your Heart in the Middle
sections.body:
The middle does something to a person if he is not watching. It breeds a particular sickness, and the sickness has a name. It is resentment dressed as discernment.

You see what could be better. You are not allowed to fix it. The gap between your sight and your authority becomes a wound, and the wound festers into a story you tell yourself about the people above you. They are blind. They are threatened by you. If only they would step aside. The story feels like clarity. It is rot.

Absalom started here. He stood at the gate, told the people their cases were just and that no one represented them, and stole the hearts of Israel one grievance at a time. He was not wrong that things could be better. He was poisoned by the conviction that he was the one being wronged, and it ended with a spear and a tree and a father weeping. The man who leads from the middle while quietly building a case against those above him is not leading. He is rehearsing a coup in his heart.

Watch for the day you start enjoying the failures of the ones in charge. That day, you have stopped serving the church and started serving your own vindication.

sections.title: Faithful in Another Man's House
sections.body:
Jesus said something about the middle that should reframe the whole thing. If you have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who will give you that which is your own.

The ministry you serve under is another man's house. The vision is his. The final call is his. And how you handle yourself inside a house you did not build is the test of whether you will ever be trusted with one of your own. God is watching how you steward authority you do not have before he decides whether to give you any.

This means the middle is not your sentence. It is your apprenticeship. Every day you serve well under leadership you would do differently, you are being formed into someone worth following. Or you are nursing the grievance that will disqualify you. There is no neutral. The middle either makes you or exposes you.

Lead where you are. Lead the things you actually control, which are more than you think and start with yourself. Be the kind of person to whom God can safely hand more. And if more never comes, be faithful in the house you are in, because that faithfulness was never really about the house. It was about you all along.
